import polars as pl

import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")




View code
it_city = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/it_cities.csv")




Questions
This notebook uses a table of 388 Italian cities, city_name, lon, lat, and pop. Every city in the table has a population over 20,000; smaller comuni were left out. lon and lat are plain numbers for now, degrees of longitude and latitude, not yet a geometry geo can work with. Most questions below build a geometry column on top of them and then use it, so unlike earlier chapters, a few answers get saved back into it_city instead of only printed, the same way the chapter itself keeps reassigning metro as it goes. Anything that is not a geometry-building step should still just be printed.

Answer: It already looks like Italy, boot and islands and all. That is a coincidence of the numbers, not a property of the plot. Longitude and latitude are being read as if they were ordinary x and y coordinates, with no geometry, no CRS, and nothing telling plotnine these points sit on a curved surface. It works here mostly because Italy is a small, mid-latitude country; the distortion this hides gets much worse for something that stretches close to the poles.

Plot that same table with geom_map() and coord_fixed(). Does it still look like Italy?



View code
(
    ggplot(
        it_city
        .with_columns(
            geometry = pl.format("POINT ({} {})", c.lat, c.lon)
        )
    )
    .geom_map()
    .coord_fixed()
)









Answer: No. The outline is rotated onto its side and mirrored, nothing like the shape from question 2. WKT points are written POINT (lon lat), longitude first, and swapping the order silently builds a valid geometry that describes the wrong locations. Nothing in the code raised an error; the map just quietly plotted something else. This is exactly why the chapter moves on to points_from_xy instead of building WKT text by hand for anything beyond a quick demonstration.

In the first block, add coord_fixed() to the plot from question 2, so its axes are locked to the same scale as a map. In the second block, project it_city into EPSG:7791, the modern reference system for Italy, and plot that with geom_map() and coord_fixed() too. Compare the two.



View code
(
    ggplot(it_city, aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
    .coord_fixed()
)











View code
(
    ggplot(it_city.geo.to_crs(7791))
    .geom_map()
    .coord_fixed()
)









Answer: With the axes locked, the two look almost the same. The chapter’s own map of the continental US, Alaska, and Hawaii shifts a lot more under projection, because it stretches from the tropics almost to the Arctic. Italy only runs from about 37°N to 47°N, a 10-degree band where a degree of longitude does not shrink by nearly as much as it does at the latitudes where the US map has real problems. The projection is still the correct thing to do, both for the reasons in the chapter’s “Why projections matter” callout and because later notebooks need it for area and distance; it just has less visible work to do on a plot this size.

Make an interactive map of it_city with .geo.explore(), showing city_name and pop in the tooltip. Zoom in on a city you already know something about and check that the map has it in the right place.



View code
it_city.geo.explore(tooltip=["city_name", "pop"])


Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook



Filter to cities with a population over 500,000, the same .filter() from several chapters back, then chain straight into .geo.explore() with the same tooltip.



View code
(
    it_city
    .filter(c.pop > 500_000)
    .geo.explore(tooltip=["city_name", "pop"])
)


Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


Six cities come back: Rome, Milan, Naples, Turin, Palermo, Genoa. That list is checkable without the map. Anyone who has seen a map of Italy already knows those are roughly its six biggest cities, in roughly that order, so a wildly wrong pin here would be obvious before trusting anything built on top of it later.

Filter to cities south of 39°N and explore the result. What part of Italy is this, and does the cluster of points on the map match what you’d expect geographically?



View code
(
    it_city
    .filter(c.lat < 39)
    .geo.explore(tooltip=["city_name", "pop"])
)


Make this Notebook Trusted to load map: File -> Trust Notebook


Answer: Sicily and the toe of Calabria on the mainland, 49 cities in total. The points bunch up around Palermo, Catania, and the Sicilian coast, with a thinner scatter across the mainland side of the strait, which is a reasonable match for where Southern Italy’s larger towns actually sit.

Answer: The smallest city in the table, Guidonia, has 20,943 people, and 86 of the 388 cities, better than one in five, sit within 5,000 of that same floor. That is not a natural break in the data; it is a cutoff someone applied when building the table. Italy has roughly 7,900 comuni in total, and this table only has 388 of them. A row missing from a spatial table is just as easy to miss as a row missing from any other kind: an empty patch on a map looks the same whether it is a real gap in the countryside or a gap in the data.

Setup
Run all of the following before starting the notebook.


View code
! wget -q -nc https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/funs.py




View code
import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"




View code
rva = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/flightsrva_flights.csv.gz", null_values=["NA"])
airline = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/flightsrva_airlines.csv.gz", null_values=["NA"])
airport = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/flightsrva_airports.csv.gz", null_values=["NA"])
plane = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/flightsrva_planes.csv.gz", null_values=["NA"])




Questions
This notebook is a review of the whole first semester: types, filtering and sorting, plotting, grouping, windows, joins, and reshaping. Nothing here is new. The dataset is four tables about commercial flights out of Richmond (RIC) in 2019. rva is the main table, one row per flight, with scheduled and actual times, delays in minutes, the carrier, the tail number of the aircraft, the destination, and the distance flown. airline maps a two-letter carrier code to a full company name. airport maps a three-letter FAA code to a name, a location, and a time zone; rva’s dest column matches airport’s faa column, not its own name. plane is a registry of individual aircraft, keyed by tailnum, with the manufacturer, model, and seat count. Print results unless a question says otherwise.
